blocks.text: Whenever work is done on a body, it increases its energy. For example, if a force F acts on a body of mass m, initially moving with velocity v_i, through a distance d and increases its velocity to v_f, then the acceleration produced will be:
From the second law of motion:

blocks.title: Tid-bits
blocks.text: All the food you eat in one day has about the same energy as 1/3 litre of petrol.

blocks.text_alt: or   Fd = ½ mv_f² − ½ mv_i²   (4.18)

blocks.text: This expression is the work-energy theorem. It states that:

blocks.title: Work-energy theorem
blocks.text: The change in kinetic energy of an object is equal to the work done on it by a net force.

blocks.text_alt: W = Change in kinetic energy = (K.E)_f − (K.E)_i = ½ mv_f² − ½ mv_i²

blocks.text: This is also known as work-energy principle.

The work-energy theorem is applicable for any direction of the force relative to the displacement. For instance, an object with kinetic energy can perform work if it is allowed to push or pull on another object. In this case, the work will be taken as negative and the kinetic energy of the object will decrease. The theorem remains valid even if the force may vary from point to point.

blocks.title: Example 4.4
blocks.problem: A motorcycle rider weighing 60 kg is coasting down a 24° slope. The weight of motorcycle is 30 kg. At the top of the slope, the speed of motorcycle is 3.2 m s⁻¹. If the kinetic frictional force is 100 N, what will be the speed of the motorcycle 72 m downhill?
steps: The normal force F_N is balanced by the component of weight (mg cos 24°) perpendicular to the slope. Let the kinetic frictional force is f, then the net force F is:
F = mg sin 24° − f   where m = total mass = 60 kg + 30 kg = 90 kg
Wok done W = Fd = 252.8 N × 72 m = 18201.6 J
As work is positive, so applying work − energy theorem, W = (K.E.)_f − (K.E.)_i
Putting the values, we have ½ mv_f² = W + ½ mv_i²
